bib.title: AppAgent: Multimodal Agents as Smartphone Users

question: Can a multimodal LLM operate arbitrary smartphone apps through GUI-level taps and swipes, learning each new app from self-exploration or human demonstrations without any fine-tuning?
hypothesis: A reference document built by exploration (autonomous or from demonstrations), plus a simplified action space with numbered UI elements, lets an off-the-shelf multimodal LLM operate unseen apps about as well as a hand-written document would.
contributions: We open-source a multimodal agent framework, focusing on operating smartphone applications with our developed action space.
We propose an innovative exploration strategy, which enables the agent to learn to use novel apps.
Through extensive experiments across multiple apps, we validate the advantages of our framework, demonstrating its potential in the realm of AI-assisted smartphone app operation.

method.summary: A GPT-4 (vision) agent on Android receives a screenshot with numbered overlays on interactive elements (from the XML) and calls a small function set (tap, long_press, swipe, text, back, exit). In an exploration phase it builds a per-app document of what each UI element does, by autonomous trial or by watching a human; in deployment it reads that document each step and does observe, think, act, summarize with a running summary as memory. Nothing is trained.
method.task: Smartphone app operation through GUI actions (high-level natural-language tasks on 10 apps)

datasets.name: Own benchmark: 10 apps (Google Maps, Twitter, Telegram, YouTube, Spotify, Yelp, Gmail, TEMU, Clock, Lightroom)
datasets.size: 50 tasks over 10 apps; Table 1 reports 45 tasks over 9 apps (Lightroom excluded)
datasets.source: Authors' own task set; task list not given in the paper

datasets.name: Lightroom case study images
datasets.size: 5 images with visual issues such as low contrast and overexposure

models.name: GPT-4 (multimodal, interleaved image and text input)

other.note: Paper says 'GPT-4' only; no version, snapshot or API name given.

inference.prompting: Per step the prompt holds the current screenshot with numbered elements, the generated document for the UI elements, explanations of all actions and a summary of history; the model outputs Observation, Thought, Action, then a summary of the step that is fed into the next prompt as memory.
inference.retrieval: Dynamically generated per-app document is supplied by looking up UI elements on the current page; retrieval mechanism not detailed.

parameters.element_id: from XML resource ID if provided, otherwise class name + size + content
parameters.exploration_stop_rule: stops when the assigned task is complete; skips pages unrelated to the app's main tasks (e.g. ads) and uses Back()

other.environment: Android OS, command-line interface; inputs are a real-time screenshot and an XML file of interactive elements
other.actions: Tap(element:int), Long_press(element:int), Swipe(element:int, direction:str, dist:str), Text(text:str), Back(), Exit()
other.action_count_discrepancy: text says 'four basic functions' but lists six
other.demo_exploration: a human operates the app and the agent records only the elements and actions the human used

metrics.name: Successful Rate (SR)
metrics.definition: average rate at which the agent completes tasks within an app; failing to finish in 10 steps counts as failure

metrics.name: Reward
metrics.definition: authors' own reward model: UI pages of each task were scored, closer to the objective scores higher, so failed runs earn credit from the final state; scale not stated

metrics.name: Average Steps
metrics.definition: average steps needed to finish tasks successfully

metrics.name: Avg. Rank (Lightroom user study)
metrics.definition: users rank edited images from the different methods; mean rank

metrics.name: Num. Tools
metrics.definition: average number of tools used for image editing

baselines: GPT-4 with no document, raw action API
GPT-4 with no document, simplified action space
eval.protocol: Single configuration per row; number of runs, seeds and user-study participants not stated; no variance or significance reported. Lightroom was excluded from the SR table because task completion is ambiguous, and evaluated by a user study ranking the outputs of 5 images.

availability.code: Open-sourced per contributions; project page https://appagent-official.github.io/ (no repo URL in text)

evidence.quote: We report the average performance of 45 tasks on 9 of the 10 previously described apps.

results.claim: The simplified action space (numbered elements) alone lifts GPT-4 with no document from near zero to roughly half of tasks.
results.setup: GPT-4, no reference document, raw action space (2.2%) versus the authors' action space (48.9%); success within 10 steps.
results.table: Table 1, rows GPT4 (Baseline) None Raw and None Ours, column SR (reward 0.6 to 3.5, avg steps 4.0 to 6.9)

results.claim: A document from autonomous exploration raises SR to 73.3%.
results.setup: AppAgent with GPT-4, document from autonomous exploration, simplified action space; reward 5.1, avg steps 4.4.
results.table: Table 1, row AppAgent Auto. Exploration, column SR

results.claim: A document from watching human demonstrations gives 84.4% SR.
results.setup: AppAgent with GPT-4, document from watching demos, simplified action space; reward 4.7, avg steps 5.1.
results.table: Table 1, row AppAgent Watching Demos, column SR

results.claim: A manually crafted document (oracle) gives 95.6% SR, the ceiling; explored documents come within about 11 to 22 points of it.
results.setup: AppAgent with GPT-4, manually crafted document, simplified action space; reward 5.5, avg steps 5.5.
results.table: Table 1, row AppAgent Manually Crafted, column SR
results.note: The table caption claims auto-generated docs yield 'outcomes on par with' manual ones, yet the gaps are 22.3 points (autonomous) and 11.2 points (demos).

results.claim: Lightroom user study: agents with a document rank better than the GPT-4 baseline, and the demo document is close to the manual one.
results.setup: Task 'fix this image until it looks good to you'; Watching Demos 1.95 vs GPT-4 baseline 2.30 vs Manually Crafted 1.75; tools used 5.8, 2.4, 4.0.
results.table: Table 2, row AppAgent Watching Demos, column Avg. Rank
results.note: Participant count and rating protocol not given; gaps are small on 5 images.

results.claim: The authors attribute the raw-action failure to the model being unable to produce accurate xy coordinates.
results.setup: Qualitative observation, no separate measurement of coordinate error.
results.quote: Our observations indicate that LLM struggles with producing accurate xy coordinates, while our simplified action space eliminates this challenging requirement.

limits: Simplified action space: 'advanced controls such as multi-touch and irregular gestures are not supported' (Limitation paragraph).
Evaluation is small and self-built: 50 tasks on 10 apps, 45 on 9 in the SR table; the task list, run count, seeds and variance are not reported, so differences have no error bars.
The reward model is described only loosely (scored UI pages per task); scale is not stated and 'Reward' ranges up to 5.5.
Lightroom is judged by an unspecified user study over 5 images and was excluded from SR because completion is ambiguous.
Only GPT-4 is used; no open-source multimodal model result, no prompt text, no GPT-4 version; the paper calls out a performance gap between open-source models and GPT-4V.
No comparison to other GUI-agent systems or trained baselines; autonomous exploration stays 22.3 points below the manual document.
Task success within 10 steps is a hard cap, and exploration is capped at 40 steps, so long tasks are untested.
Safety, privacy, error recovery and cost are not measured, though the intro claims better security and privacy by avoiding back-end access.
